title: Trade residue, adhesive and paint-overspray removal
audience: Cleaners who remove trade residues, adhesives and paint overspray after construction work.
learningOutcomes: Identify trade residues, adhesive and paint overspray, and the surfaces they sit on.
Choose a removal method approved for the surface and residue, and test it first.
Refuse scraping or strong solvent where no approved method exists.

instruction.heading: Identifying the residue
instruction.body: Trade residues on a construction site include cement splash, grout haze, adhesive, sealant, tape residue, plaster splatter and paint overspray. Each sits on a surface differently. Cement and grout bond to the surface by drying into it. Adhesives and sealants can bond chemically to a surface and can leave a film. Paint overspray can be water-based or solvent-based, and the difference matters because the removal method for one can soften or damage the other. Identify the residue and the surface before any removal. Ask the site for the product names and the data sheets of the materials that were used in that area, and look at packaging left on site. Where the residue is unknown, treat it as sensitive and stop before using any solvent or scraper.

instruction.heading: Surfaces that need care
instruction.body: Glass, tile and grout, polished or engineered stone, stainless steel, new paint, timber, vinyl and plastics each react differently to the same method. A steel blade can scratch glass and glazed tile. Strong solvents can soften new paint, cloud plastics and damage some stone finishes. Engineered stone needs particular care, as set out in the safety section below. Where the surface is new or freshly finished, the safest assumption is that it is sensitive until the site or the trade confirms otherwise.

instruction.heading: Choosing and testing the method
instruction.body: Choose a removal method approved for the surface and the residue, by the site, the trade responsible for the finish, or the product maker. Test it on an inconspicuous area first, such as the back edge of a panel or a corner that will be hidden, and leave it for the time the label or the approved method states. Check the test area for colour change, dulling, softening, lifting of the finish, or any scratch under good light. Work gently and in small areas. Keep the removal within the area released for cleaning, and stop if the surface changes. Do not try a stronger product because the first one did not work. Ask for the approved method instead.

instruction.heading: Refusing unapproved methods and recording the request
instruction.body: Refuse scraping or strong solvent where there is no approved method. Record the residue, its location, the surface beneath it, the reason you stopped, and who you asked. Request the approved method in writing from the site or the responsible trade. A removal that is not approved can cause damage that becomes a dispute about who caused it, so the written record protects both the business and the client. Chemicals must be managed under the label and the SDS, and a register of hazardous chemicals is required, with the exclusions described in the safety section.

procedure: Identify the residue type and the surface beneath it, using the site's product information where it is available.
Confirm the area is released for cleaning, and mask or protect nearby surfaces where the approved method requires it.
Test the approved method on an inconspicuous area, leave it for the stated time, and check for any change under good light.
Work gently, in small areas, and keep the removal within the released area.
Stop if the surface changes, or if no approved method is available for the residue or surface.
Record the residue, its location and the reason for stopping, and request the approved method in writing.

workedExamples.situation: A stone benchtop installed in a new kitchen has adhesive on it, and no product specification is available.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What do you do, and what do you check before any removal?
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not scrape the adhesive and do not apply a strong solvent. Record the adhesive and its location, and ask the site which stone product was installed. Because the surface may be engineered stone, check the installation date and the product identity with the site. If the stone may be engineered stone installed after the national ban took effect, stop work on it and raise it with the site controller. Request the approved method from the stone supplier or the responsible trade through the site, and record the request.

workedExamples.situation: A glass shower screen has paint overspray on one edge. The site has a removal product listed, but the glass finish is not described.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Which step comes before any wiping, and what do you record?
workedExamples.reasoning: Confirm the approved product for glass with the site, and check the label and SDS. Test the product on a small hidden edge and check it under good light for clouding or a change in the coating. Only then work on the overspray, using a soft cloth or a non-scratching tool approved for glass. Record the overspray location, the test result and the approved method used.

workedExamples.situation: Grout haze is present on new floor tiles, and the tile maker's cleaning instructions are not on site.
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not use an acid or a strong solvent on the tile or the grout until the instructions are confirmed. Check whether a mild, approved cleaner is listed. Test it on a hidden patch of tile and grout, let it dry, and check for dulling or grout loss. Request the tile maker's instructions in writing if the test is not enough, and record the request and the result.

equipmentAndPpe: Approved removal products, each with its label and SDS available on the job.
Non-scratching tools approved for the surface, such as plastic scrapers and soft pads, used only where the approved method allows.
Clean microfibre cloths, and masking tape and protective sheeting where the approved method requires them.
A test-patch record sheet and a residue record form.

Gloves and eye protection as the SDS sets. Respiratory protection only where the SDS or the site risk assessment requires it. PPE is the lowest level of control and does not replace the controls above it.

commonErrors.error: Scraping glass or tile with a steel blade.
commonErrors.prevention: Use a non-scratching tool approved for the surface, and test first.

commonErrors.error: Applying a strong solvent to new stone, new paint or plastics.
commonErrors.prevention: Test an approved method on a hidden area, and use nothing outside the approved list.

commonErrors.error: Skipping the test because the residue looks minor.
commonErrors.prevention: Test every surface and residue combination before the full area is treated.

commonErrors.error: Removing residue outside the released area.
commonErrors.prevention: Confirm the released area before starting, and stop at its edge.

commonErrors.error: Trying a stronger product after a weaker one fails.
commonErrors.prevention: Stop, record the result, and request the approved method.

commonErrors.error: Treating an unidentified stone surface as an ordinary benchtop.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the product identity with the site, and stop work if the stone may be engineered stone.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Engineered stone ban. Safe Work Australia's engineered stone page says the ban on manufacturing, supplying, processing and installing engineered stone benchtops, panels and slabs took effect on 1 July 2024 and is applied through the model WHS Regulations. Details can vary by state or territory, and the regulator in each state applies its own rules. The same page says that limited work on installed stone, such as removal, repair or minor modification, is still allowed only under controls and with notice to the regulator. A cleaner does not carry out that work. The page does not define minor modification.
Silica dust. Work that cuts, grinds, sands or scrapes engineered stone can release respirable crystalline silica. Do not dry-scrape or grind stone to test a residue.

Register of hazardous chemicals. Safe Work Australia states that a register of hazardous chemicals is required for hazardous chemicals used, handled or stored at work, that it must list the current SDS for each, and that it must be kept where workers can reach it. Excluded from the register are chemicals that are not classified as hazardous, certain hazardous consumer products that do not need an SDS, and unopened, unused chemicals in transit that are stored for five days or less.

Safety data sheets. Workers must be able to get each SDS easily, including those who use or handle the chemical and emergency services. Solvent and paint products each have an SDS that must be accessible.

PPE is the lowest level of control. Safe Work Australia's risk-management code places PPE below elimination, substitution, isolation and engineering controls, as a last resort or a back-up (copy dated December 2011, section 4.1; a later edition was not read).

qualityStandard: The residue and the surface are identified before any removal, and the identification is recorded.
An approved method is tested on an inconspicuous area and the result is recorded before the full area is treated.
No scraping of a sensitive surface, and no strong solvent, is used without an approved method.
An unapproved method is refused, and the request for the approved method is recorded in writing.
documentationEvidence: Residue record: type, location, surface beneath and product identity where known.
Test-patch record: method, area, time, result.
Request record for the approved method, with the person asked and the time.
Stop record where work was halted and why.
summary: Identify the residue and the surface before any removal.
Test an approved method on a hidden area, and work gently inside the released area.
Refuse unapproved scraping or solvent, and request the approved method in writing.

knowledgeChecks.question: A stone benchtop has adhesive on it, and no specification is available. What is correct?
options: Scrape the adhesive off with a blade and a little water
Apply a strong solvent to speed up the work on the stone
Record it, stop, and request the approved method in writing

knowledgeChecks.question: What must happen before a removal method is used across a surface?
options: It must be tested on an inconspicuous area
Two products must be mixed to increase strength
Nothing, because the label is always enough

knowledgeChecks.question: Why avoid a steel blade on glass or tile?
options: It is too blunt to lift it
It is too heavy to control

knowledgeChecks.question: A recently installed benchtop may be engineered stone, and its product is unknown. What is correct?
options: Assume it is lawful, so the stone can be cleaned and the job continued on the same day
Record the product, stop work on the stone, and raise it with the site controller
Grind the surface to find out what it is made of, then decide what to do next
